title: Imani's Light Balance
markdown:
Rain hammered the shelter roof. Thunder boomed close enough to make the tin shiver. Inside it was dark, the kind of dark that makes you count the seconds between flashes. “The main light’s dead,” Engineer Imani announced, already kneeling by the junction box. Priya tapped the bulb. Cold glass. Rune the crow cawed, curious, and hopped onto a crate as if he had been promoted to inspector.

Imani grabbed a hand-crank generator from the emergency kit, the one with the worn handle and a label that had given up being readable. “Electricity’s like water,” she said, voice steady against the weather. “The crank is the push — the voltage. The wires carry it.” She cranked. Whirr. A tiny test bulb flickered, weak as a shy star. “Not enough.” She cranked harder. WHIRRR. The bulb brightened, then sulked again when she eased off.

She twisted a dial on the little board she had clipped in. Click. The light died.

“Whoa. You killed it,” Priya yelped.

“Not killed. Squeezed too hard.” Imani turned the dial back. Click. The light flickered again, a moth deciding. With one hand cranking and the other guiding the dial, she hunted a sweet spot — not all push, not all squeeze. The bulb settled into a steady warm glow. Rain still hammered. The room had a centre again. Rune cawed as if he had done the maths.

“A balance,” Imani said, eyes bright. “Voltage is the push. The dial is resistance. Too much resistance, the light fades. Too little, and you dump the push with nothing useful to show. The brightness you see is the current — the flow.”

Priya’s mind raced. She watched the crank, the dial, the glow, three things arguing and then agreeing. “So a big push needs just the right squeeze to get a strong flow.”

“That’s Ohm’s Law. Voltage, resistance, current. They have to work together or the bulb sulks and the crank is just exercise.”

They found the perfect balance for this bulb, this rain, this tired generator. Imani marked the dial with a pencil tick so the night shift would not twist it to heroic and burn the filament. Priya did not spring up ready for whatever the day would bring. She sat on the crate beside Rune, watched the warm circle on the floor, and counted how many cranks kept the glow honest before her arm complained. Imani took the next turn without making a speech about rules being only the start. The thunder moved off a little. The light stayed.
